messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Arthur, a 73-year-old divorced journalist, still remembers the taste of smoke and burnt metal that filled his mouth as he stood among the wreckage of the collapsed convention center. He had arrived early to photograph the aftermath of the deliberately set explosion—a man-made disaster that killed 27 people—and the image he captured of a child’s shoe half-buried in debris won an award he can no longer bear to look at. Every time his phone buzzes with a news alert, his throat tightens. When he scrolls past a photograph of any disaster—even a house fire in another state—the event replays in his mind like a film he cannot stop, and for a moment he feels the heat on his skin and hears the screams again, as if he is right there. The memory feels so extreme that he sometimes tells himself it could not have really happened to him, yet his body reacts as if it is happening now.

Arthur has come to believe that if he lets himself think about the explosion, he will completely lose control and never recover the ability to feel normal again. This belief has hollowed out his days; nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, and he spends impulsively on new cameras, lenses, and online subscriptions—anything to distract from the gap where purpose used to be. That compulsive spending, however, often leads him back to the exact photos he was trying to avoid, because his credit card statements remind him of the equipment he used that day. He now sits only with his back to the wall in restaurants and coffee shops, scanning every face that enters. He listens for sounds that might mean someone is forcing his apartment door, even though he lives on the fifteenth floor. In any room he notices potential weapons—a letter opener, a fire extinguisher, a heavy ashtray—and he cannot relax even when he knows he is safe.

When an unfamiliar taste touches his tongue—something metallic, or the acrid tang of burnt wiring—Arthur’s mind snaps back to the explosion site, and the unreality of the memory deepens: he freezes completely where he stands, unable to move or speak until the taste fades. He is aware that this freezing only makes the memory more vivid when it returns, because the fear of the next unpredictable trigger becomes a constant hum in his body. He monitors for any sound that might signal an intruder, and his hypervigilance often leads him to re-experience the disaster, because his racing heart and scanning eyes mirror the panic he felt that day. His compulsive spending, too, has a way of circling back: after buying something he does not need, he feels a brief relief that quickly dissolves into shame, and the shame reinforces his conviction that he will never feel normal emotions again. That belief, in turn, makes it harder for him to sit with the memory, so he avoids it more intensely, and the avoidance only confirms that the memory is too dangerous to face.

Arthur has stopped accepting assignments that involve unpredictable locations or crowds. He works from home now, filing stories by email, but even there, the taste of his morning coffee sometimes carries an echo of smoke, and he finds himself checking his window locks three times before he can concentrate. His ex-wife stopped calling years ago; his children send texts he rarely answers. What finally brought him to the clinic was a week during which he could not leave his apartment because every time he stepped outside, a car backfired or a siren wailed, and he felt the pavement shake beneath him. He is terrified that his mind is slipping away, but what he hopes—though he can barely admit it—is that someone can convince him the memory is real, and that he can survive it.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals influence or trigger the memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory causes the patient to perceive or encounter triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the perceived threat causes triggers to appear or be noticed.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Arthur has come to believe that if he lets himself think about the explosion, he will completely lose control and never recover the ability to feel normal again.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That certainty that he could not handle it kept pulling him back into the moment itself, as if his mind needed to test whether this time he would finally shatter, and the memory came sharper each time he told himself it was too dangerous.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
the unreality of the memory deepens: he freezes completely where he stands, unable to move or speak until the taste fades.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After one of those episodes, Arthur would find himself noticing every unusual smell in his apartment—burnt toast, bleach, a neighbor’s cooking oil—as though the world had become covered in clues he could not afford to miss.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In any room he notices potential weapons—a letter opener, a fire extinguisher, a heavy ashtray—and he cannot relax even when he knows he is safe.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling this hunted all the time had become the most convincing evidence he had that his life was permanently broken, that the person he used to be was gone for good.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He listens for sounds that might mean someone is forcing his apartment door, even though he lives on the fifteenth floor.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That constant hum of danger turned ordinary background noises—a neighbor’s footsteps, the elevator chime, a distant shout—into things that made him stiffen and search for what was wrong.
